option_explanations.A: The shift from 'gunboat diplomacy' to 'dollar diplomacy' came later, under Taft — using financial power rather than warships in the Caribbean. The Philippine war was gunboat diplomacy's product, not dollar diplomacy's beginning.
option_explanations.B: The event began no isolation — it began the opposite: the era of overseas American empire. Isolation from world affairs was the 1920s–30s story, not 1899's.
option_explanations.C: 'Brinkmanship' to détente is Cold War vocabulary (Dulles to Kissinger/Nixon) — half a century later and about nuclear rivalry with the Soviets, not about the Philippines.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The Philippine-American War (1899–1902) opened the era in which the United States held overseas colonies — the Philippines, Puerto Rico, Guam — marking a new imperial phase in American foreign policy: the moment the republic became, in the anti-imperialists' charge, an empire.

items.explanation: Hakluyt marvels that after 'so great conquests and plantings of the Spaniards and Portuguese' in the ninety years since discovery, England had no foothold in 'such fertile and temperate places as are left as yet unpossessed.' His motive is competitive and mercantilist: Spain and Portugal were growing rich from America, and England risked being shut out of the colonial race.
options: (A) Opposition to the power of the English monarchy.
(B) Concern for the welfare of Native American peoples.
(C) A desire to carry Protestantism to the peoples of Asia.
(D) Envy of Spanish and Portuguese colonial wealth and fear that England would be left behind.
items.stem: Hakluyt's lament that England had never 'set fast footing' in America was driven chiefly by which of the following?
items.stimulus: "I marvel not a little . . . that since the first discovery of America (which is now full four score and ten years), after so great conquests and plantings of the Spaniards and Portuguese there, that we of England could never have the grace to set fast footing in such fertile and temperate places as are left as yet unpossessed of them. . . . I conceive great hope that the time approacheth . . . that we of England may share and part stakes (if we will ourselves) both with the Spaniard and the Portuguese in part of America . . ." — Richard Hakluyt, Divers Voyages Touching the Discovery of America, 1582

option_explanations.A: Hakluyt did not oppose the English monarchy — he wrote to promote English national glory under the crown, urging the queen's government to sponsor colonization. His lament is patriotic, not anti-monarchical.
option_explanations.B: Concern for Native welfare is nowhere in Hakluyt's lament — his 'fertile and temperate places' are valued for what England can take from them, not for the wellbeing of their inhabitants. His motive is competitive, not humanitarian.
option_explanations.C: Carrying Protestantism to Asia was not Hakluyt's project — his eyes were on America, and his argument was about English wealth and power, not missionary work in the East.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Hakluyt marvels that in the ninety years since discovery, after 'so great conquests and plantings of the Spaniards and Portuguese,' England had never managed 'to set fast footing' in the 'fertile and temperate places' still unpossessed. His motive is competitive and mercantilist: Spain and Portugal were growing rich on American wealth while England watched — and England would be left behind unless it colonized too.

items.explanation: Hakluyt's propaganda helped inspire the English colonizing ventures that produced Jamestown (1607) and the subsequent Atlantic-coast colonies.
options: (A) drive the French and Portuguese governments into bankruptcy.
(B) conquer large parts of Africa during the eighteenth century.
(C) establish colonies along North America's Atlantic coast.
(D) destroy the Dutch commercial empire.
items.stem: Pursuing Hakluyt's ideas, England eventually managed to

option_explanations.A: England did not drive France and Portugal into bankruptcy — both remained great powers for centuries. Hakluyt's propaganda produced colonies, not the financial ruin of rivals.
option_explanations.B: England did not conquer large parts of Africa in the eighteenth century — the Scramble for Africa came in the late nineteenth. Hakluyt's legacy was American, not African.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Hakluyt's promotional writings helped inspire the English colonizing ventures that produced Jamestown (1607) and the subsequent Atlantic-coast colonies — the 'fast footing' in America he had lamented England's lack of.
option_explanations.D: England did not destroy the Dutch commercial empire — the Anglo-Dutch wars of the 1600s hurt Dutch trade but left the Netherlands a major commercial power. Hakluyt's program was about building England up in America, not about destroying Holland.

items.explanation: 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God' (1741) — with its image of God holding the sinner 'much as one holds a spider... over the fire' — is the signature sermon of the First Great Awakening, the 1730s–1740s evangelical revivals in which Edwards and George Whitefield preached human depravity and the urgent need for conversion.
options: (A) The Second Great Awakening.
(B) Transcendentalism.
(C) The Social Gospel movement.
(D) The First Great Awakening.
items.stem: Edwards's sermon is a landmark text of which of the following?
items.stimulus: "The God that holds you over the pit of hell, much as one holds a spider, or some loathsome insect, over the fire, abhors you, and is dreadfully provoked. . . . You have offended him infinitely more than ever a stubborn rebel did his prince: and yet 'tis nothing but his hand that holds you from falling into the fire every moment." — Jonathan Edwards, 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God,' 1741

option_explanations.A: The Second Great Awakening was the early-1800s revival movement (Finney, camp meetings) — a century after Edwards. Edwards's 1741 sermon belongs to the first wave, not the second.
option_explanations.B: Transcendentalism (Emerson, Thoreau, 1830s–40s) celebrated individual intuition and nature's divinity — the opposite of Edwards's vision of depraved sinners dangling over hell by God's mere will.
option_explanations.C: The Social Gospel (late 1800s) applied Christian ethics to social reform — poverty, labor, inequality. Edwards's sermon is about personal damnation and divine wrath, not social reform.
option_explanations.D: Correct. 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God' (1741) — with its unforgettable image of God holding the sinner 'much as one holds a spider, or some loathsome insect, over the fire' — is the signature sermon of the First Great Awakening, the 1730s–40s evangelical revivals in which Edwards and George Whitefield preached human depravity and the urgent need for conversion.

items.explanation: Edwards's 1741 sermon is the iconic text of the First Great Awakening (1730s–1740s), the evangelical revival that swept the colonies with itinerant preaching and emotional conversion.
options: (A) Transcendentalism and its celebration of individual intuition
(B) Mormonism
(C) the Great Awakening
(D) the Social Gospel
items.stem: Edwards's sermon was a central text of

option_explanations.A: Transcendentalism celebrated individual intuition as the path to truth — Edwards's sermon preaches the opposite: that human intuitions are corrupt, reason is no defense, and only God's arbitrary mercy keeps sinners from hell.
option_explanations.B: Mormonism began in the 1830s with Joseph Smith — a new scripture and a new church, a century after Edwards and a different religious movement entirely.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Edwards's 1741 sermon is the iconic text of the First Great Awakening (1730s–40s) — the evangelical revival that swept the colonies with itinerant preaching, emotional conversions, and the doctrine that every soul stood in immediate peril.
option_explanations.D: The Social Gospel was the late-1800s movement applying Christianity to industrial-era social problems. Edwards's hellfire sermon is about individual salvation and divine wrath, not social reform.

items.explanation: Edwards preached amid the spiritual complacency of 1730s New England; the Awakening's revivals were a deliberate effort to rekindle piety among colonists whom ministers saw as backsliding.
options: (A) piety had declined in Puritan New England, and he sought to rekindle religious fervor.
(B) Massachusetts had disestablished the Congregational Church, forcing itinerant preaching.
(C) New England had absorbed waves of Catholic, Jewish, Protestant, and nonbelieving immigrants whom Edwards hoped to convert.
(D) recent war with Native peoples had shaken survivors' faith in God.
items.stem: Edwards preached in a context in which

option_explanations.A: Correct. Edwards preached amid the spiritual complacency of 1730s New England — the Half-Way Covenant era, when ministers lamented backsliding and declining piety. The Awakening's revivals were a deliberate effort to rekindle religious fervor among colonists whom the clergy saw as growing cold.
option_explanations.B: Massachusetts did not disestablish the Congregational Church until 1833 — a century after Edwards. In his day the church was established and settled ministers were the norm; itinerant preaching was the Awakening's innovation, not a response to disestablishment.
option_explanations.C: New England in the 1730s–40s had absorbed no such immigrant waves — the great Catholic, Jewish, and freethinking immigrations came in the nineteenth century. Edwards preached to the grandchildren of Puritans, not to newcomers.
option_explanations.D: No recent Native war had shaken survivors' faith in Edwards's context — his Northampton congregation's crisis was spiritual coldness, not war trauma. The sermon addresses complacency, not catastrophe.

items.explanation: The Awakening's emphasis on personal conversion and individual religious judgment eroded deference to established authority and gave ordinary colonists a new, inward sense of self — transformations in how they understood God, themselves, and the world.
options: (A) encouraging colonists to question and challenge the legitimacy of British authorities.
(B) denouncing slavery's immorality and demanding its end.
(C) promoting amicable relations with Native peoples.
(D) reshaping colonists' understandings of God, themselves, and the world.
items.stem: The broader movement Edwards belonged to changed colonial society by

option_explanations.A: The Awakening did not directly encourage colonists to challenge British authority — any political spillover (a more individualistic, anti-deferential spirit) was indirect and debated. The movement's direct transformation was religious and personal, not imperial-political.
option_explanations.B: The Awakening did not denounce slavery or demand its end — George Whitefield, the movement's great itinerant, actually owned enslaved people and defended the institution in Georgia. Abolition was not the Awakening's fruit.
option_explanations.C: The movement did not promote amicable Native relations — its energies were directed at colonial souls, and the era's frontier warfare continued unabated. Indian policy was untouched by the revivals.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The Awakening's emphasis on personal conversion and individual religious judgment reshaped how colonists understood God (sovereign and terrifyingly immediate), themselves (sinners capable of direct spiritual experience), and the world (a stage for salvation, not merely a parish hierarchy). It eroded deference to established authority and gave ordinary colonists a new inward sense of self.

items.explanation: The Ford ad markets the car not as a novelty but as an attainable status possession — the 1920s pattern in which installment credit and mass production put automobiles, radios, and appliances within ordinary families' reach.
options: (A) Consumer safety as manufacturers' chief concern
(B) Automobiles as rare luxuries affordable to few
(C) unproven new technologies requiring extensive propaganda to attract skeptical consumers.
(D) Mass-produced goods as affordable status symbols
items.stem: The advertisement best illustrates which feature of the 1920s?
items.stimulus: Image description: Ford Motor Company advertisement, 1926 — a polished magazine ad presenting the automobile as a stylish, desirable possession for ordinary families.

option_explanations.A: Consumer safety was not manufacturers' chief concern in the 1920s — Ralph Nader'sUnsafe at Any Speed was forty years away. The Ford ad sells style and desirability, not safety engineering.
option_explanations.B: Automobiles were not rare luxuries by 1926 — the Model T had been in mass production since 1908, and millions of Americans owned cars. The ad presents the car as an attainable possession for ordinary families, not an aristocratic rarity.
option_explanations.C: The automobile was not an unproven novelty needing propaganda to win skeptics in 1926 — it was an established, mass-produced product. The ad is selling status and style within an already-converted market, not pioneering acceptance.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The 1926 Ford ad markets the car not as a novelty but as an attainable status possession — the 1920s pattern in which installment credit and mass production put automobiles, radios, and appliances within ordinary families' reach, turning manufactured goods into markers of modern middle-class life.

items.explanation: Installment buying — 'buy now, pay later' — let 1920s consumers spread the cost of cars, radios, and appliances over time, fueling the decade's consumer boom and its household-debt overhang.
options: (A) installment payment plans spreading the cost over time.
(B) self-assembly kits that lowered the seller's costs.
(C) exclusive retail stores that kept consumers from buying at the lowest possible price.
(D) rebates earned by selling products for the manufacturer.
items.stem: Like radios and appliances, automobiles were commonly sold through

option_explanations.A: Correct. Installment buying — 'buy now, pay later' — let 1920s consumers spread the cost of cars, radios, and appliances over months and years. Credit, not cash, fueled the decade's consumer boom — and left the household-debt overhang that made the Depression's collapse so devastating.
option_explanations.B: Self-assembly kits were not how cars and appliances were sold — Ford sold finished automobiles through dealers, and appliance makers sold finished goods through stores. The cost savings came from the assembly line, not from customer labor.
option_explanations.C: Exclusive retail stores keeping prices high is the opposite of the 1920s pattern — chain stores, mail order, and installment credit were driving prices down and access up, not restricting it.
option_explanations.D: Rebates earned by selling products for the manufacturer describes a salesman's commission scheme, not how consumers bought cars. Ordinary families bought on installment plans, not by becoming agents.

items.explanation: The 1920s consumer economy grew directly out of industrial mass production — the assembly line, electrification, and entrepreneurial marketing that made goods cheap, standardized, and widely available.
options: (A) Manifest Destiny and territorial expansion
(B) the Industrial Revolution and entrepreneurial innovation.
(C) Reconstruction and southern 'Redemption.'
(D) World War I and the era's new spirit of international cooperation.
items.stem: The 1920s consumer economy most directly built on

option_explanations.A: Manifest Destiny and territorial expansion belonged to the mid-1800s — the continental filling. The 1920s consumer economy was built on factories and credit, not on new territory.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The 1920s consumer economy grew directly out of industrial mass production — the assembly line, electrification, and entrepreneurial marketing that made goods cheap, standardized, and widely available. Ford's moving assembly line (1913) is the technological ancestor of the 1920s showroom.
option_explanations.C: Reconstruction and southern 'Redemption' (1860s–70s) were about the postwar South's political order — they have no connection to the 1920s consumer boom.
option_explanations.D: World War I's 'spirit of international cooperation' collapsed with the Senate's rejection of the League — and the consumer economy was a domestic industrial phenomenon, not a product of wartime internationalism.

items.explanation: Mechanized reapers, steel plows, and millions of new cultivated acres flooded markets with grain and cotton after the Civil War; chronic surpluses drove the farm-price deflation the index records.
options: (A) the growth of family farms in the 1870s and 1880s as thousands of 'new immigrant' families settled the rural Midwest.
(B) Population stagnation from birth control and a growing middle class
(C) Agricultural mechanization and expanded acreage creating surpluses
(D) Latin American surpluses flooding U.S. markets
items.stem: Which best explains the price trend shown in the table?

option_explanations.A: The growth of family farms settled by 'new immigrant' families misreads the migration — the 'new immigrants' of the 1870s–90s went overwhelmingly to industrial cities, not to Midwestern farms. And more farms would not by itself explain the relentless price decline.
option_explanations.B: Population did not stagnate — it grew rapidly through immigration and natural increase, and birth control was not yet a demographic force. Growing population should have raised demand and prices, not lowered them; this gets the mechanism backward.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Mechanized reapers, steel plows, and millions of new cultivated acres flooded markets with grain and cotton after the Civil War. Chronic surpluses — too much wheat, too much cotton chasing too little demand — drove the farm-price deflation the index records: from 140 in 1866 to 56 in 1896.
option_explanations.D: Latin American surpluses did not flood U.S. markets in this era — the United States was itself the great surplus producer, exporting grain and cotton to the world. The glut was American-grown.

items.explanation: The Populist Omaha Platform (1892) demanded 'free and unlimited coinage of silver' to inflate the currency and lift farm prices — the movement's signature monetary demand against the gold standard's deflation.
options: (A) a national sales tax.
(B) government funding for farm machinery.
(C) federal 'internal improvements' in the West, including railroads and canals.
(D) an end to the gold standard and coinage of silver.
items.stem: To address the conditions in the table, Populists demanded

option_explanations.A: A national sales tax is regressive — it would have hurt farmers, not helped them. The Populists demanded inflationary money and government credit, not a tax on consumption.
option_explanations.B: Government funding for farm machinery was never the Populist demand — their program was monetary (free silver), credit (the subtreasury plan), and structural (railroad regulation, income tax). Machinery subsidies were not on the Omaha Platform.
option_explanations.C: Federal 'internal improvements' — railroads and canals — were the old Whig/Republican program, and railroads were the Populists' enemy, not their demand. The movement wanted to regulate the railroads, not build them more.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The Populist Omaha Platform (1892) demanded 'free and unlimited coinage of silver' — an end to the gold standard's deflationary discipline — to inflate the currency, lift farm prices, and ease farmers' debts. It was the movement's signature monetary demand: more money, higher prices, lighter debts.

items.explanation: Falling prices pushed farmers into the Grange, Farmers' Alliances, and cooperatives — local and regional networks built to fight railroad rates, middlemen, and corporate control of agricultural markets.
options: (A) the creation of federal agencies overseeing farm production and limiting output.
(B) Lower tariffs to stimulate trade and cut surpluses
(C) Farmers organizing networks to resist corporate market control
(D) Big producers building a transcontinental railroad
items.stem: The trend in the table helped prompt which development of the era?

option_explanations.A: Federal agencies overseeing farm production and limiting output came with the New Deal's Agricultural Adjustment Act (1933) — four decades later and a different philosophy (government management rather than farmer self-organization).
option_explanations.B: Lower tariffs to cut surpluses was not the farmers' answer — tariffs were a Republican sacred cow, and farmers' problem was overproduction at home, not foreign competition. Their demands were monetary and organizational, not tariff-based.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Falling prices pushed farmers into the Grange, the Farmers' Alliances, and cooperatives — local and regional networks built to fight railroad rates, middlemen, and corporate control of agricultural markets. Organization was the farmers' answer to a market that individually they could not move.
option_explanations.D: Big producers did not build a transcontinental railroad — the railroads were built by corporations with massive federal land grants and subsidies, and farmers regarded them as exploiters, not allies. The railroad was the problem, not the farmers' project.
